title: Restart and first detection in a lackadaisical quantum walk with flat-band localization
abstract: We study stochastic and sharp restart in a one-dimensional lackadaisical discrete-time quantum walk with self-loop weight $\ell$. In the absence of restart, the dynamics has a flat band responsible for intrinsic localization and two dispersive bands supporting ballistic propagation. We compare two initially localized benchmark states: a flat-band-active state with finite flat-band overlap and a flat-band-dark state with zero flat-band overlap. For geometric stochastic restart with per-step restart probability $q$, the stationary mean-squared displacement scales as $q^{-2}$ as $q\to0$. In the same limit, the restart-site occupation probability approaches the restart-free intrinsic localized value for the flat-band-active state, whereas for the flat-band-dark state it vanishes as $q\ln(1/q)$. For power-law restart, where $p_m\propto m^{-s}$ is the probability that the waiting time to the next restart is $m$ steps, a normalized stationary site-occupation distribution exists only for $s>2$, while the stationary absolute spatial moment of order $p$ is finite only for $s>p+2$. In the regime $1<s\leq2$, at every fixed lattice site, the flat-band-active occupation converges to the intrinsic flat-band profile, while the flat-band-dark occupation tends to zero. We also consider monitored first detection with sharp restart, in which the walk is reinitialized after a fixed number $r$ of consecutive unsuccessful measurements. For fixed $r$, the mean first-detected-passage time of the flat-band-active state exhibits a minimum at an intermediate self-loop weight, whereas the flat-band-dark state approaches a ballistic detection limit as $\ell\to\infty$.
summary: This paper analyzes a quantum walk model to separate intrinsic spectral localization from confinement effects induced by external 'restart' mechanisms. By studying geometric and power-law restarts, the authors derive scaling laws for transport observables like the mean-squared displacement. The results demonstrate that the restart process acts as a spectral discriminator, allowing the recovery of the intrinsic localized state even when the walk is perturbed.
main_problem: The study investigates how different restart mechanisms (stochastic or sharp) affect the long-time spatial localization and transport properties of a quantum walk.
main_result: The analysis distinguishes between intrinsic spectral localization (flat band) and confinement due to the restart process, showing distinct scaling behaviors for different initial states.
method: The research employs spectral decomposition of the quantum walk propagator and analyzes the asymptotic behavior of site-occupation probabilities and mean-squared displacement under renewal processes.
model_or_system: The model is a one-dimensional lackadaisical discrete-time quantum walk (LDTQW) defined on a lattice, characterized by a self-loop weight $\ell$. The dynamics are analyzed by decomposing the evolution into contributions from an intrinsically localized flat band and dispersive bands.
key_observables: Mean-squared displacement ($\langle x^2 angle$), restart-site occupation probability, stationary site-occupation distribution, and mean first-detected-passage time.
important_parameters: Restart probability ($q$) for geometric restart, power-law exponent ($s$) for power-law restart, and the self-loop weight ($\ell$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on taking limits such as $q 	o 0$ or $t 	o \infty$ to characterize the long-time steady states.
paper_structure: The paper systematically builds the analysis by first establishing the restart-free dynamics, then developing the renewal formalism for stochastic restarts (geometric and power-law), and finally analyzing the specific case of monitored first detection.
why_interesting: The work provides a rigorous framework for understanding how external measurement or resetting processes modify fundamental quantum transport phenomena, which is relevant for open quantum systems and quantum measurement theory.
